# 1\. Executive Summary

Plan My Marriage will be implemented as a TypeScript Next.js modular monolith. The same deployable application serves authenticated planning workflows, the public wedding website, token-protected guest experiences, and backend Route Handlers. MongoDB Atlas is the system of record, Mongoose is the data-access layer, Cloudflare R2 stores wedding media, Cloudflare CDN serves gallery assets through a custom media domain, and Resend sends transactional invitations.

The architecture is intentionally stateless at the application tier. Authenticated users use a signed HttpOnly cookie session; wedding authorization is determined by WeddingMember records. Guests do not receive accounts. Instead, high-entropy capability tokens grant narrow access to invitation, RSVP or event-photo-upload workflows. Raw tokens are never stored in the database; only SHA-256 hashes are persisted.

Images upload directly from the browser to Cloudflare R2 using short-lived presigned PUT URLs. This avoids moving large photo payloads through the Next.js server and is particularly important when many guests upload photos concurrently from a QR code during an event. Photo metadata remains in MongoDB, while object bytes remain in R2.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 1. High-level system context and external dependencies._

# 2\. Scope, Goals and Non-Goals

## 2.1 Goals

- Provide one coherent architecture for the PRD-approved V1 feature set.
- Keep deployment and operations simple enough for a single developer while supporting a serious production product.
- Enforce wedding-level data isolation and role-based authorization for Admins and Managers.
- Allow accountless guests to RSVP and upload event photos securely through scoped tokens.
- Support image-heavy wedding galleries without routing image bytes through the application server.
- Keep external integrations behind adapters so providers can be changed later.
- Make horizontal application scaling possible without redesigning authentication or state management.

## 2.2 Non-Goals

- Microservices or service mesh architecture.
- Kafka, message brokers or event sourcing.
- Redis as a mandatory V1 dependency.
- Kubernetes or container orchestration.
- A separate Express backend.
- Real-time WebSocket collaboration.
- Native video streaming infrastructure.
- Payment processing, subscriptions or vendor marketplace transactions.
- AI features in the initial architecture.

## 2.3 Initial design assumptions

| **Dimension**     | **Design assumption (not a hard product limit)**                        |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Wedding size      | Up to about 1,000 guests and 25 events per wedding                      |
| Gallery           | Up to about 5,000 photos per wedding in early production                |
| Upload burst      | Tens to roughly 100 concurrent guest uploads during an event            |
| Application scale | Up to roughly 10,000 active weddings before architecture review         |
| Photo formats     | JPEG, PNG and WebP in V1; HEIC requires an explicit conversion strategy |
| Photo size        | Configurable limit; recommended initial maximum 10 MB per image         |

# 3\. Architecture Decisions

| **Area**              | **Decision**                               | **Rationale**                                                                           |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Architecture          | Modular monolith                           | Fast to build and operate; clean domain boundaries without distributed-system overhead. |
| Application framework | Next.js, TypeScript                        | One full-stack codebase for UI, server rendering and backend Route Handlers.            |
| Database              | MongoDB Atlas                              | Managed MongoDB cluster; good fit for document-oriented wedding data.                   |
| ODM                   | Mongoose                                   | Central schemas, indexes, validation hooks and consistent data access.                  |
| Validation            | Zod                                        | Shared request/form schemas; server validation remains authoritative.                   |
| Media storage         | Cloudflare R2                              | Object storage for image-heavy gallery data with S3-compatible APIs.                    |
| Media delivery        | Cloudflare CDN on custom media domain      | Edge caching for guest-facing gallery assets.                                           |
| Email                 | Resend                                     | Transactional manager and guest invitation emails.                                      |
| App authentication    | Signed HttpOnly cookie session             | Simple browser auth; no localStorage bearer token.                                      |
| Guest access          | Random capability tokens                   | No guest account while preserving narrow, revocable access.                             |
| Rate limiting         | MongoDB-backed fixed-window limiter for V1 | Distributed across app instances without introducing Redis.                             |
| Deployment            | Recommended: Vercel for Next.js            | Simple Next.js hosting; not a hard architectural dependency.                            |

**Provider independence:** The architecture depends on capabilities, not vendor-specific UI. The Next.js host, vendor-search provider and rate-limit backend can be replaced later without changing domain models.

# 4\. System Context

Admins and Managers use the authenticated planning surface. Guests use either the public wedding site or a token-protected experience. The monolith owns business rules and metadata, but delegates durable storage of media to R2 and transactional delivery of emails to Resend.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 2. System context (repeated here as the reference context diagram)._

## 4.1 Trust boundaries

| **Boundary**              | **Trusted identity**                | **Allowed capabilities**                                        |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Authenticated application | Signed user session + WeddingMember | Planning actions for weddings where user is a member.           |
| Public wedding website    | None                                | Read only data intentionally published through /w/:slug.        |
| Guest invitation          | Valid guest capability token        | Read invitation context and update RSVP for that guest only.    |
| Event photo upload        | Valid event upload token            | Request upload URLs and add photos only to one wedding event.   |
| R2 direct upload          | Short-lived presigned PUT URL       | Upload one object key with constrained content type and expiry. |

# 5\. Application Surfaces

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 3. Explicit separation of the three product surfaces._

## 5.1 Surface 1 - /app/\*

All routes under /app/\* require an authenticated user session. This surface contains the planning dashboard, events, tasks, expenses, guests, vendors, gallery management, team management and settings. Route protection happens before page data is returned, and every wedding-specific mutation performs a server-side membership check.

```
/app/dashboard
/app/events
/app/tasks
/app/expenses
/app/guests
/app/vendors
/app/gallery
/app/team
/app/settings
```

## 5.2 Surface 2 - /w/:slug

The public wedding website requires no login. It returns only data considered publishable for the wedding website. It must never expose internal task, expense, member, token or invitation records. The slug is human-friendly and unique, but it is not a security credential.

## 5.3 Surface 3 - token-protected guest experience

Guests do not create accounts. Invitation and photo-upload routes are guarded by high-entropy tokens. The token is a capability: possession grants a limited operation, not general wedding access. Recommended namespaces are /guest/invite/:token and /guest/upload/:token, with matching /api/v1/guest/\* backend routes.

**Important:** Public wedding URLs and guest tokens solve different problems. A public slug identifies a wedding; a capability token authorizes a specific guest or event operation.

# 6\. Modular Monolith Design

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 4. Internal layering of the Next.js modular monolith._

## 6.1 Domain modules

| **Module**         | **Responsibilities**                                             |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Auth               | Register, login, logout, session verification, password hashing. |
| Weddings           | Wedding profile, slug, theme, public website configuration.      |
| Members            | Admin/Manager membership, manager invitation and removal.        |
| Events             | Ceremonies, venue, dates, livestream URL.                        |
| Tasks              | Task CRUD, assignment, status and priorities.                    |
| Expenses           | Simple expense log and aggregates.                               |
| Guests             | Guest records, guest groups and event assignment.                |
| Invitations / RSVP | Guest access tokens, email/share links and event-level RSVP.     |
| Gallery            | Photo metadata, R2 presigning, finalize and deletion.            |
| Themes             | Classic Indian, Modern Minimal and Royal Indian rendering.       |
| Vendors            | Provider-agnostic vendor search adapter.                         |
| Email              | Resend adapter and transactional templates.                      |
| Rate Limit         | Fixed-window policy and storage abstraction.                     |

## 6.2 Layering rule

Route Handlers should remain thin. They parse the request, authenticate/token-check, apply rate limits, validate with Zod and call a domain service. Domain services implement business rules and authorization. Mongoose models/repositories handle persistence. External adapters isolate R2, Resend and vendor APIs.

```
HTTP / Server Action
    -> auth or guest-token guard
    -> rate-limit policy
    -> Zod schema
    -> domain service
    -> repository / external adapter
    -> response
```

# 7\. Deployment Topology

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 5. Recommended production deployment topology._

## 7.1 Next.js hosting

Vercel is the recommended first host because it minimizes operational overhead for Next.js. The design deliberately avoids Vercel-only domain logic, so the application can later move to another Node.js-compatible platform. Database access, R2 access and Resend calls must execute in the Node.js runtime rather than relying on edge-only assumptions.

## 7.2 Media domain

Use a dedicated custom domain such as media.planmymarriage.com for gallery reads. The domain is attached to the R2 bucket so Cloudflare Cache can serve images from edge locations. The r2.dev development endpoint should not be used for production gallery delivery.

## 7.3 DNS

- planmymarriage.com and application subdomains point to the Next.js host.
- media.planmymarriage.com points to the Cloudflare R2 custom domain / cache path.
- The sending domain is verified with Resend using the required DNS records.
- MongoDB Atlas remains private to application credentials and network rules; clients never connect directly.

# 8\. Routing and API Conventions

Use versioned JSON APIs for client-side mutations and guest actions. Server Components may call domain services directly for server-rendered reads when convenient, but business logic must not be duplicated between pages and API handlers.

| **Route family** | **Example**                         | **Protection**                                |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Auth             | /api/v1/auth/login                  | Public + strict rate limit                    |
| Planning         | /api/v1/weddings/:weddingId/events  | Authenticated + membership                    |
| Public           | /api/v1/public/weddings/:slug       | Public read-only                              |
| Guest invitation | /api/v1/guest/invite/:token/context | Token-protected                               |
| Guest RSVP       | /api/v1/guest/invite/:token/rsvp    | Token-protected + rate limit                  |
| Photo upload     | /api/v1/guest/upload/:token/presign | Token-protected + strict rate limit           |
| Media finalize   | /api/v1/media/finalize              | Authenticated or guest token depending source |

## 8.1 Response envelope

```
Success:
{ "data": { ... }, "requestId": "..." }

Error:
{
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
    "message": "Please check the highlighted fields.",
    "details": { ... }
  },
  "requestId": "..."
}
```

## 8.2 HTTP semantics

- GET for reads; POST for creation/actions; PATCH for partial updates; DELETE for deletions.
- Use 400 for validation, 401 for unauthenticated, 403 for authenticated-but-not-authorized, 404 for missing/inaccessible resources, 409 for uniqueness/state conflicts, 429 for rate limit and 5xx for server/provider failures.
- Do not disclose whether a wedding/resource exists when doing so would leak cross-wedding information; return a consistent not-found response.

# 9\. Authentication and Authorization

## 9.1 User authentication

V1 uses email/password authentication. Passwords are stored using an adaptive salted password hash. Successful login issues a signed session token in a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax cookie. The browser never stores the session in localStorage. Logout clears the cookie.

The session payload should remain small: userId, issuedAt, expiry and a sessionVersion. A sessionVersion field on User allows global invalidation after password/security changes without maintaining a separate session store.

## 9.2 Wedding authorization

Roles are not stored as a single field on User. They belong to the User-to-Wedding relationship through WeddingMember. This supports one person being an ADMIN in one wedding and a MANAGER in another.

```
WeddingMember
- weddingId
- userId
- role: ADMIN | MANAGER
- joinedAt

Unique index: (weddingId, userId)
```

## 9.3 Request flow

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 6. Authenticated API request authorization flow._

## 9.4 Admin-only actions

- Remove a Manager.
- Ownership-sensitive wedding settings and destructive controls.
- Future actions that change membership or ownership boundaries.

**Security rule:** Every wedding-scoped query must derive or verify weddingId on the server. Never trust a client-provided role and never authorize by hiding UI controls alone.

# 10\. Token-Protected Guest Access

## 10.1 Token format and storage

Generate at least 256 bits of cryptographically secure randomness and encode it in a URL-safe format. Send the raw token only to the intended link. Store SHA-256(token) in MongoDB, not the raw token. On request, hash the presented token and perform an indexed lookup.

## 10.2 Token types

| **Token**             | **Scope**                                                     | **Typical lifetime**                                    | **Revocation**               |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| GuestAccessToken      | One guest, one wedding; invitation + RSVP for assigned events | Through wedding period plus a configurable grace period | Set revokedAt / status       |
| PhotoUploadToken      | One event; request photo upload URLs                          | Event window plus configurable grace period             | Set revokedAt / rotate token |
| MemberInvitationToken | One invited email and wedding role                            | Short, e.g. 7 days                                      | Accepted, expired or revoked |

## 10.3 Token rules

- Tokens are bearer capabilities and must never appear in application logs or analytics payloads.
- Comparison uses tokenHash lookups; database snapshots do not reveal usable links.
- Tokens are scoped to the minimum data and action needed.
- Expired or revoked tokens return a generic invalid/expired-link screen.
- Photo-upload QR codes use event upload tokens, not guest RSVP tokens.

# 11\. Email Invitation Architecture

Resend handles transactional emails only. Plan My Marriage does not build campaign marketing, newsletters or an email queue in V1.

## 11.1 Manager invitation

**1\.** Admin enters the Manager email address.

**2\.** Server validates membership rules and creates a MemberInvitation with a hashed random token and expiry.

**3\.** Resend sends an invitation URL containing the raw token.

**4\.** Recipient signs in or creates an account.

**5\.** Accept endpoint validates token and email, creates WeddingMember and marks invitation accepted.

**6\.** The create-membership and accept-invitation state change should use a MongoDB transaction.

## 11.2 Guest invitation

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 7. Guest email invitation and RSVP flow._

Each invited guest can receive a unique guest link. WhatsApp sharing and Copy Link may reuse the same guest URL. The organizer-facing Guest Group remains an organizational construct; V1 does not require shared household login or a family-level account.

## 11.3 Delivery handling

- Store invitation sentAt and optional provider messageId for operational visibility.
- If Resend returns an immediate error, surface a retryable UI error; do not mark the invitation sent.
- Protect send endpoints with per-user/per-wedding rate limits to prevent abuse and accidental repeated sends.
- Use a verified sending domain and consistent From/Reply-To configuration.

# 12\. Media, Gallery and QR Upload Architecture

R2 stores all binary images. MongoDB stores only metadata such as weddingId, eventId, objectKey, source and timestamps. A photo is associated with an event when applicable; a wedding-level image such as a cover can have no eventId or a separate media purpose field.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 8. Direct-to-R2 upload and CDN gallery delivery._

## 12.1 Upload flow

**1\.** Browser requests a presigned upload URL from Next.js.

**2\.** Server authenticates the user or validates the event photo token.

**3\.** Rate limiter checks the applicable policy.

**4\.** Zod validates metadata such as event, file name, MIME type and declared size.

**5\.** Server generates a random object key and a short-lived R2 presigned PUT URL.

**6\.** Browser uploads the bytes directly to R2.

**7\.** Browser calls finalize with the object key.

**8\.** Server performs an R2 HEAD request, verifies actual content length/type and ownership prefix, then creates Photo metadata.

**9\.** Gallery reads metadata from MongoDB and renders CDN URLs derived from the object key.

## 12.2 Object key strategy

```
weddings/{weddingId}/covers/{uuid}.{ext}
weddings/{weddingId}/events/{eventId}/photos/{uuid}.{ext}
weddings/{weddingId}/events/{eventId}/guest-photos/{uuid}.{ext}
```

Never use the original file name as the authoritative object key. User file names may be stored as metadata for display, but random keys prevent collisions and reduce information leakage.

## 12.3 QR upload

Each event can create or rotate one PhotoUploadToken. The QR code encodes the token-protected guest upload URL. A scanned QR never exposes an Admin/Manager session and grants no access outside that event upload capability.

## 12.4 Upload constraints

| **Control**      | **V1 behavior**                                                                  |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Allowed formats  | JPEG, PNG, WebP initially                                                        |
| Size             | Configurable; recommended 10 MB maximum per image                                |
| Presign expiry   | Short-lived; recommended 5-15 minutes                                            |
| Finalization     | Required before photo becomes visible in MongoDB-backed gallery                  |
| Invalid upload   | Reject metadata; delete object when practical                                    |
| Guest moderation | Admin/Manager can delete unwanted photos; no complex approval workflow initially |

# 13\. Cloudflare R2 and CDN Strategy

## 13.1 Read path

Attach a custom domain to the R2 bucket for gallery reads. Cloudflare documents that caching for R2 is enabled through a custom domain; the r2.dev development URL does not provide the same cache/WAF behavior. The gallery application should therefore render media URLs from a configured CDN base such as <https://media.planmymarriage.com/{objectKey}>.

## 13.2 Write path

Presigned uploads use the R2 S3-compatible endpoint, not the custom CDN domain. Cloudflare R2 supports presigned PUT URLs through its S3-compatible API. The application generates these URLs server-side with R2 credentials and never sends long-lived R2 credentials to the browser.

## 13.3 Public-read implication

A custom domain attached directly to R2 makes those object paths publicly reachable if known. This matches the current PRD because wedding gallery images are guest-facing content. Sensitive documents must never be stored in this public media path. If a future premium/private gallery requires access control, add signed read URLs or a Worker/WAF authorization layer without changing photo metadata.

# 14\. Validation and Rate Limiting

## 14.1 Zod

All external input is validated with Zod at the server boundary. Client-side form reuse improves UX, but server validation is authoritative because public/token endpoints can be called directly.

| **Schema example**  | **Purpose**                                        |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| RegisterSchema      | Email, password, display name                      |
| CreateWeddingSchema | Bride/groom names, wedding date, city, theme       |
| CreateEventSchema   | Name, date/time, venue and description             |
| TaskSchema          | Assignment, priority, status and due date          |
| ExpenseSchema       | Category, amount, date and optional event          |
| GuestSchema         | Name, optional email/phone/group                   |
| RSVPSchema          | Allowed RSVP state for invited event IDs           |
| UploadRequestSchema | Event, MIME type, file size and file name metadata |

## 14.2 Rate limiter architecture

V1 uses a MongoDB-backed fixed-window limiter so multiple Next.js instances share a consistent counter without adding Redis. A RateLimitBucket document is atomically incremented with findOneAndUpdate/upsert. A TTL index removes expired buckets. The limiter is wrapped behind an interface so it can later move to Redis or an edge provider without changing routes.

```
RateLimitBucket
_id: hash(policy + identity + windowStart)
count: number
expiresAt: date   // TTL index

identity examples:
- login: normalized IP + normalized email
- guest RSVP: IP + token fingerprint
- photo upload: IP + event-token fingerprint
- invite sending: userId + weddingId
```

## 14.3 Suggested policies

| **Endpoint type**        | **Relative policy**                                 |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Login / register         | Strict                                              |
| Guest RSVP               | Moderate; enough for retries but resistant to spam  |
| Photo presign/finalize   | Strict per token and IP, with small burst allowance |
| Send invitation email    | Strict per user/wedding                             |
| Authenticated CRUD reads | Generous                                            |
| Vendor search            | Moderate to control third-party API cost            |

**Future scale:** If rate-limit traffic becomes a meaningful share of MongoDB workload, replace the storage adapter with Redis/Upstash or an edge/WAF limiter. No domain change is required.

# 15\. Domain Data Model

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 9. High-level MongoDB entity relationships._

## 15.1 Multi-tenancy model

Plan My Marriage is a logical multi-tenant system with Wedding as the tenant boundary. Most domain records carry weddingId. Every authenticated wedding-scoped query includes weddingId together with resource ID, which prevents IDOR-style cross-wedding access when combined with membership authorization.

## 15.2 Guest RSVP modeling

Use EventGuest as the many-to-many join between Event and Guest. It records that a guest is invited to an event and holds RSVP status. This avoids embedding large guest arrays in Event and avoids separate RSVP documents for the simple V1 response model.

```
EventGuest
- weddingId
- eventId
- guestId
- rsvpStatus: PENDING | ATTENDING | NOT_ATTENDING
- respondedAt?

Unique index: (eventId, guestId)
```

## 15.3 Gallery modeling

A separate Gallery collection is unnecessary for V1. The wedding gallery is a query over Photo records, grouped by event. This keeps the model small and aligns with the product requirement that albums correspond primarily to ceremonies.

# 16\. MongoDB Collections and Indexes

| **Collection**    | **Purpose**                      | **Key indexes**                                                       |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| users             | Unique email; sessionVersion     | { email: 1 } unique                                                   |
| weddings          | Wedding profile, slug, theme     | { slug: 1 } unique; { date: 1 }                                       |
| weddingMembers    | User role within wedding         | { weddingId: 1, userId: 1 } unique; { userId: 1 }                     |
| memberInvitations | Invite Manager by email          | { tokenHash: 1 } unique; { expiresAt: 1 } TTL                         |
| events            | Wedding ceremonies               | { weddingId: 1, date: 1 }                                             |
| tasks             | Planning tasks                   | { weddingId: 1, status: 1, dueDate: 1 }; { assignedTo: 1, status: 1 } |
| expenses          | Simple expense records           | { weddingId: 1, date: -1 }; { weddingId: 1, category: 1 }             |
| guestGroups       | Organizer-defined guest grouping | { weddingId: 1, name: 1 }                                             |
| guests            | Master guest list                | { weddingId: 1, name: 1 }; { weddingId: 1, email: 1 }                 |
| eventGuests       | Invitation + RSVP relation       | { eventId: 1, guestId: 1 } unique; { guestId: 1 }                     |
| guestAccessTokens | Guest invitation capability      | { tokenHash: 1 } unique; { guestId: 1 }                               |
| photoUploadTokens | Event photo capability           | { tokenHash: 1 } unique; { eventId: 1 }                               |
| photos            | Media metadata                   | { weddingId: 1, eventId: 1, createdAt: -1 }; { objectKey: 1 } unique  |
| rateLimitBuckets  | Fixed-window counters            | { expiresAt: 1 } TTL                                                  |

## 16.1 Index discipline

- Create indexes intentionally from actual query patterns; do not index every field.
- Prefix tenant queries with weddingId where practical.
- Use unique compound indexes for relationship integrity.
- Review Atlas slow-query insights before adding new indexes.
- Avoid unbounded arrays in Wedding or Event documents for guests/photos; use separate collections.

# 17\. Core Request and Sequence Flows

## 17.1 Create task

```
Browser -> POST /api/v1/weddings/{weddingId}/tasks
        -> verify session cookie
        -> load WeddingMember
        -> rate limit (generous authenticated policy)
        -> Zod TaskSchema
        -> TaskService.create()
        -> validate assignee belongs to same wedding
        -> MongoDB insert
        -> return 201
```

## 17.2 Guest RSVP

```
Guest -> /guest/invite/{token}
      -> hash token
      -> find active GuestAccessToken
      -> load guest + EventGuest invitations
      -> render invitation context

Guest -> POST RSVP
      -> rate limit by IP + token fingerprint
      -> Zod RSVP schema
      -> verify submitted event IDs are assigned to guest
      -> update EventGuest rows
      -> return updated RSVP state
```

## 17.3 Guest event photo upload

```
QR -> /guest/upload/{eventToken}
   -> validate event token
   -> choose images
   -> request presigned PUT URLs
   -> browser PUTs directly to R2
   -> finalize each object
   -> Photo metadata saved
   -> gallery reads through Cloudflare CDN
```

## 17.4 Manager invitation

```
Admin -> invite manager email
      -> create MemberInvitation(tokenHash, expiry)
      -> Resend email with raw token URL
Recipient -> sign in / register
          -> accept invitation
          -> transaction: create WeddingMember + mark invitation accepted
```

# 18\. Security Design

| **Threat / concern**         | **Control**                                                                                                                          |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Cross-wedding data access    | Membership check + weddingId-scoped queries on every protected resource.                                                             |
| Credential theft             | Adaptive password hashing; Secure HttpOnly cookie; secrets server-side only.                                                         |
| CSRF on cookie-auth APIs     | SameSite=Lax plus Origin/Host validation for state-changing requests; add explicit CSRF token if future cross-site flows require it. |
| Guest token database leak    | Store only SHA-256 token hashes.                                                                                                     |
| Token brute force            | 256-bit randomness + rate limiting.                                                                                                  |
| Invitation abuse             | Per-user/wedding send limits and audit fields.                                                                                       |
| Malicious file upload        | Allowlist image MIME/types, final HEAD verification, size limit, random object keys.                                                 |
| Direct R2 credential leakage | Only server owns R2 API credentials; browser gets short-lived presigned URL.                                                         |
| XSS                          | Render user text as escaped text; do not accept raw HTML in V1.                                                                      |
| NoSQL injection              | Zod schemas, explicit query construction, never pass arbitrary client objects into Mongo operators.                                  |
| Sensitive logs               | Never log passwords, raw session tokens, raw guest tokens or R2 presigned URLs.                                                      |

## 18.1 Least privilege

- Create R2 credentials scoped only to the required bucket and operations.
- MongoDB application user receives only required database permissions.
- Resend key stays server-side.
- Guest tokens encode no trusted authorization data themselves; authorization comes from database token records.
- Admin and Manager differences are enforced in domain services, not only route/UI code.

# 19\. Reliability, Error Handling and Idempotency

## 19.1 Error categories

| **Category**               | **Behavior**                                                                |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Validation                 | Return 400 with field-safe details.                                         |
| Authentication             | 401 and redirect to login for app pages.                                    |
| Authorization              | 403 or 404 depending information-leak risk.                                 |
| Provider failure           | Return retryable error; do not write success state before provider success. |
| Database transient failure | Return 503/500 with requestId; platform may retry safe reads.               |
| Expired token              | Show friendly invalid/expired link page.                                    |
| Upload finalize failure    | Keep object hidden because no Photo metadata exists; allow client retry.    |

## 19.2 Idempotency

- RSVP writes are naturally idempotent because setting the same status repeatedly produces the same result.
- Photo finalize endpoint uses objectKey uniqueness so repeated finalization does not create duplicate Photo rows.
- Manager invitation acceptance uses unique (weddingId, userId) membership and a transaction.
- Email send itself is not assumed exactly-once; UI should avoid accidental double clicks and the server should enforce short resend cooldowns.

## 19.3 Transactions

Use MongoDB transactions only for multi-document invariants that genuinely require atomicity, such as accepting a Manager invitation. Routine CRUD remains single-document or independently recoverable to keep the system simple.

# 20\. Performance and Scalability

## 20.1 Application tier

The application tier is stateless because sessions are signed cookies and shared mutable state lives in MongoDB/R2. Multiple Next.js instances can therefore serve traffic without sticky sessions. Connection reuse is required for Mongoose to avoid excessive Atlas connections in serverless environments.

## 20.2 Gallery

- Direct-to-R2 uploads remove large request bodies from Next.js.
- Cloudflare CDN absorbs repeated gallery reads.
- Use lazy loading and responsive image sizes on gallery pages.
- Paginate or cursor-load Photo metadata rather than returning thousands of records in one response.
- Use random object keys and immutable cache headers for versioned photo objects where practical.

## 20.3 Database

- Compound indexes reflect wedding-scoped query patterns.
- Use aggregation for expense/category summaries only where needed; avoid expensive dashboard work on every request when simple grouped queries suffice.
- Keep documents bounded; guests, photos, tasks and event assignments remain separate collections.
- Review Atlas metrics and slow query profiler before introducing caching.

## 20.4 When to revisit architecture

| **Signal**                                             | **Likely next step**                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Rate-limit collection becomes significant DB load      | Move limiter storage to Redis/edge rate limiting.                |
| Vendor API cost/latency is high                        | Add TTL cache for provider results.                              |
| Private media becomes a requirement                    | Add signed read/Worker/WAF layer.                                |
| Image transformations become necessary                 | Add Cloudflare Images/transform pipeline or dedicated processor. |
| Long-running/bulk email workflows appear               | Add background job/queue.                                        |
| One module scales independently by orders of magnitude | Evaluate extraction from monolith only then.                     |

# 21\. Observability and Operations

## 21.1 Structured logging

Emit structured server logs with requestId, route, method, status, duration, userId when authenticated, weddingId where applicable, and provider error category. Never log raw access tokens, passwords, session cookies or presigned URLs.

## 21.2 Metrics to watch

- API latency and 5xx rate by route family.
- Authentication failures and rate-limit hits.
- MongoDB connection count, query latency and slow queries.
- R2 presign/finalize failures and upload completion rate.
- Resend send failures.
- Guest RSVP submission success rate.
- Photo upload success/failure and average object size.

## 21.3 Error reporting

Start with deployment-platform logs and request IDs. A dedicated error tracker such as Sentry can be added later if production usage justifies it; the architecture does not require it for V1.

# 22\. Configuration and Secrets

| **Variable / secret**        | **Purpose**                                                   |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| MONGODB_URI                  | MongoDB Atlas connection string                               |
| SESSION_SECRET               | Signs authenticated session tokens                            |
| APP_BASE_URL                 | Canonical application URL                                     |
| R2_ACCOUNT_ID                | Cloudflare account identifier                                 |
| R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID             | R2 S3-compatible credential                                   |
| R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY         | R2 S3-compatible secret                                       |
| R2_BUCKET_NAME               | Media bucket                                                  |
| MEDIA_CDN_BASE_URL           | e.g. <https://media.planmymarriage.com>                       |
| RESEND_API_KEY               | Transactional email API key                                   |
| EMAIL_FROM                   | Verified sender                                               |
| VENDOR_PROVIDER_KEY          | Vendor/places provider key if selected                        |
| MAX_IMAGE_BYTES              | Upload size policy                                            |
| TOKEN_HASH_PEPPER (optional) | Optional server-side defense-in-depth for stored token hashes |

Secrets belong in the deployment secret store and local .env files excluded from source control. Public environment variables must contain no credentials.

# 23\. Testing Strategy

| **Layer**              | **What to test**                                                                                                |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Unit                   | Domain services, role rules, token hashing, object-key generation, validation helpers.                          |
| Repository/integration | Mongoose indexes, membership queries, EventGuest uniqueness, TTL behavior.                                      |
| API integration        | Auth, authorization, Zod errors, rate limits, guest token boundaries.                                           |
| Provider contract      | R2 presign/finalize with test bucket; Resend sandbox/test behavior; vendor adapter.                             |
| End-to-end             | Create wedding -> add event -> add guest -> invite -> RSVP -> QR photo upload -> gallery.                       |
| Security               | Cross-wedding ID tampering, revoked tokens, expired tokens, malicious upload metadata, repeated login attempts. |

## 23.1 Critical E2E scenarios

**1\.** Admin creates wedding and invites a Manager; Manager joins and can access the same wedding.

**2\.** Manager cannot remove an Admin.

**3\.** A user from Wedding A cannot read or mutate Wedding B by changing IDs.

**4\.** Guest invitation token reveals only that guest's invitation context and assigned events.

**5\.** Guest can RSVP and dashboard reflects the new EventGuest statuses.

**6\.** Event QR token can upload to that event but cannot modify RSVP or access planning APIs.

**7\.** Guest image uploads directly to R2, finalizes, and appears through the CDN gallery.

**8\.** Revoked token stops working immediately at the application layer.

# 24\. Failure Modes and Recovery

| **Failure**                            | **User-visible behavior**                         | **Recovery**                                             |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| MongoDB unavailable                    | Planning/RSVP unavailable; friendly retry message | Retry after Atlas recovers; no local fallback writes.    |
| R2 presign unavailable                 | Photo upload temporarily unavailable              | Retry presign; other app functions continue.             |
| R2 upload interrupted                  | Client shows failed photo and retry               | Request a new presigned URL.                             |
| Finalize fails after successful R2 PUT | Photo not shown in gallery                        | Retry finalize; periodic/manual orphan cleanup later.    |
| Cloudflare CDN issue                   | Images may load slowly/fail while metadata works  | Fallback can use R2 path operationally; investigate CDN. |
| Resend unavailable                     | Invitation send fails clearly                     | Retry later; existing invitation links remain valid.     |
| Vendor API unavailable                 | Vendor search unavailable only                    | Core wedding planning remains functional.                |

## 24.1 Backups

Production should use a MongoDB Atlas tier with backups enabled. R2 is the source of truth for photo bytes; accidental deletion protection/versioning should be evaluated before monetization or high-value production use. Destructive wedding deletion should require explicit confirmation and can later become a delayed/soft-delete workflow.

# 25\. Evolution Path

The architecture intentionally creates seams where scale or premium requirements can be added without rewriting the product.

| **Future requirement**               | **Evolution path**                                                             |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Premium plans / payments             | Add billing module and provider adapter; no change to wedding core.            |
| AI assistant                         | Add AI module that reads authorized wedding data through domain services.      |
| Private gallery                      | Change media read layer to signed URLs / Worker / WAF; Photo model remains.    |
| Image optimization / HEIC conversion | Add asynchronous transformation pipeline or Cloudflare image product.          |
| Automated WhatsApp                   | Add messaging adapter and background jobs; existing guest tokens/links remain. |
| Heavy email campaigns                | Queue email jobs and process asynchronously.                                   |
| Mobile app                           | Reuse versioned APIs and token/session concepts.                               |
| High-scale rate limiting             | Swap MongoDB limiter adapter for Redis/edge provider.                          |

# 26\. Implementation Order

**1\.** Foundation: Next.js TypeScript project, environment config, Mongoose connection, Zod and shared error model.

**2\.** Authentication: User registration/login/logout, signed cookie session, protected /app shell.

**3\.** Wedding + membership: Wedding, WeddingMember, manager invitation via Resend.

**4\.** Events and dashboard basics.

**5\.** Tasks and simple expenses.

**6\.** Guests, Guest Groups and EventGuest assignment.

**7\.** GuestAccessToken, email invitation and RSVP surface.

**8\.** Public /w/:slug wedding site and theme renderer.

**9\.** R2 media adapter, authenticated image upload and CDN gallery.

**10\.** PhotoUploadToken, QR generation and guest direct upload.

**11\.** Vendor provider adapter.

**12\.** Operational hardening: rate limits, structured logs, security tests, backup checks and production configuration.

**Build strategy:** Deliver vertical slices that are usable end-to-end. Avoid building every database model first and every UI screen later; complete one flow at a time.

# 27\. Architecture Decision Record Summary

| **ADR** | **Decision**                                                   | **Status**                  |
| ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| ADR-001 | Use a modular monolith rather than microservices.              | Accepted                    |
| ADR-002 | Use Next.js + TypeScript as full-stack framework.              | Accepted                    |
| ADR-003 | Use MongoDB Atlas + Mongoose as primary database layer.        | Accepted                    |
| ADR-004 | Separate /app/\*, /w/:slug and token-protected guest surfaces. | Accepted                    |
| ADR-005 | Model roles using WeddingMember, not User.role.                | Accepted                    |
| ADR-006 | Guests are domain records, not authenticated users.            | Accepted                    |
| ADR-007 | Use Cloudflare R2 for media and direct browser uploads.        | Accepted                    |
| ADR-008 | Use Cloudflare CDN custom domain for gallery reads.            | Accepted                    |
| ADR-009 | Use Resend for transactional invitations.                      | Accepted                    |
| ADR-010 | Use Zod at all external input boundaries.                      | Accepted                    |
| ADR-011 | Use MongoDB-backed fixed-window rate limits initially.         | Accepted for V1             |
| ADR-012 | Use signed HttpOnly cookie session for authenticated APIs.     | Architecture recommendation |
| ADR-013 | Recommend Vercel for first deployment; keep host replaceable.  | Architecture recommendation |

| **Method**   | **Route**                                   | **Protection**       | **Purpose**                       |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| POST         | /api/v1/auth/register                       | Public               | Create user                       |
| POST         | /api/v1/auth/login                          | Public + strict RL   | Create session cookie             |
| POST         | /api/v1/auth/logout                         | Session              | Clear session                     |
| GET          | /api/v1/auth/me                             | Session              | Current user                      |
| POST         | /api/v1/weddings                            | Session              | Create wedding + ADMIN membership |
| GET/PATCH    | /api/v1/weddings/:id                        | Member               | Read/update wedding               |
| POST         | /api/v1/weddings/:id/member-invitations     | ADMIN                | Invite Manager via Resend         |
| POST         | /api/v1/member-invitations/:token/accept    | Session + token      | Accept Manager invitation         |
| GET/POST     | /api/v1/weddings/:id/events                 | Member               | List/create events                |
| PATCH/DELETE | /api/v1/weddings/:id/events/:eventId        | Member               | Update/delete event               |
| GET/POST     | /api/v1/weddings/:id/tasks                  | Member               | Task CRUD entry                   |
| GET/POST     | /api/v1/weddings/:id/expenses               | Member               | Expense CRUD entry                |
| GET/POST     | /api/v1/weddings/:id/guests                 | Member               | Guest CRUD entry                  |
| POST         | /api/v1/weddings/:id/guests/:guestId/invite | Member + RL          | Create/send guest link            |
| GET          | /api/v1/public/weddings/:slug               | Public               | Wedding website data              |
| GET          | /api/v1/guest/invite/:token/context         | Guest token          | Invitation context                |
| PUT          | /api/v1/guest/invite/:token/rsvp            | Guest token + RL     | Update event RSVP                 |
| POST         | /api/v1/weddings/:id/media/presign          | Member               | Presign authenticated upload      |
| POST         | /api/v1/guest/upload/:token/presign         | Photo token + RL     | Presign guest photo upload        |
| POST         | /api/v1/media/finalize                      | Member or capability | Verify object and create metadata |
| DELETE       | /api/v1/weddings/:id/photos/:photoId        | Member               | Delete photo metadata + object    |
| GET          | /api/v1/vendors/search                      | Member + RL          | Proxy vendor provider search      |

```
src/
```

Inside each module, prefer a predictable separation such as schema.ts (Zod), service.ts (business logic), repository.ts (persistence where useful), types.ts and tests. Avoid a global services folder that mixes unrelated domains.
